title: Secure Network Design
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 4: Communication and Network Security: Secure Network Design.

items: Divides network into smaller, isolated segments
Limits lateral movement after a breach
Reduces attack surface within each segment
Implemented through firewalls, VLANs, and subnets
Supports zero trust architecture through micro-segmentation
Demilitarized Zone — Segment between external and internal networks
Hosts public-facing services (web servers, email gateways, DNS)
Protected by two firewalls (external-facing and internal-facing)
External firewall allows specific traffic to DMZ; internal firewall restricts DMZ-to-LAN
Compromise of DMZ server does NOT give direct access to internal network

blocks.text: Dual-Firewall DMZ Architecture: `` Internet → [External Firewall] → DMZ → [Internal Firewall] → LAN `` The external firewall permits specific inbound traffic (HTTP/HTTPS to web server). The internal firewall is more restrictive, allowing only necessary communication from DMZ to internal resources (e.g., database queries on specific ports). ⚠️ Exam Trap: A DMZ with two firewalls from DIFFERENT vendors provides better defense in depth. A vulnerability in one vendor's firewall is unlikely to exist in the other vendor's product.

items: Virtual LAN — Logically separates network segments on the same switch
Creates separate broadcast domains without additional hardware
Configured on managed switches (Layer 2)
VLAN hopping — Attack that jumps between VLANs (double tagging, switch spoofing)
VLANs are NOT a security boundary alone — use with firewalls/ACLs
Disable unused ports and assign to an unused VLAN
Change the native VLAN from the default (VLAN 1)
Use 802.1Q trunking with explicit VLAN tagging
Enable port security to limit MAC addresses per port
Don't rely on VLANs as the sole security control

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: VLANs provide LOGICAL separation, not PHYSICAL separation. VLAN hopping attacks (double tagging, switch spoofing) can bypass VLAN boundaries. Always pair VLANs with ACLs and firewalls.

items: NAC (802.1X) — Controls device access to the network
Verifies identity, health, and compliance before granting access
Supplicant (client) → Authenticator (switch/AP) → Authentication Server (RADIUS)
Non-compliant devices sent to remediation VLAN
Supports BYOD security and guest network access
SDN — Separates control plane from data plane
Control plane — Decision-making (routing logic, managed centrally)
Data plane — Traffic forwarding (switches, routers)
Enables programmable, dynamic network management
Security concern: centralized controller is a single point of failure/attack
FCoE (Fibre Channel over Ethernet) — Carries storage traffic over Ethernet networks
iSCSI (Internet Small Computer System Interface) — Carries SCSI storage commands over IP networks
VoIP (Voice over IP) — Carries voice traffic over IP; uses SIP/RTP protocols
MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) — High-performance traffic routing using labels
Convergence introduces new attack surfaces — storage, voice, and data on same network

rows: Storage traffic exposed to network attacks; no native encryption
Vulnerable to IP-based attacks; must use IPsec or CHAP auth
Eavesdropping, caller ID spoofing, toll fraud, DoS

items: RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) — carries voice data; no encryption
SRTP (Secure RTP) — encrypted version; provides confidentiality and authentication
VoIP requires QoS to ensure voice quality — attackers can degrade QoS to disrupt calls

blocks.text: From Chapple: "Other concepts that may be considered examples of converged technologies include VPN, SDN, cloud, virtualization, SOA, microservices, and serverless architecture." ⚠️ Exam Trap: Converged protocols combine multiple types of traffic (storage, voice, data) onto a single network. This creates risk because a compromise of the shared network can affect ALL services. The exam tests whether you understand the security implications of convergence, particularly with VoIP (eavesdropping via packet capture) and iSCSI (storage traffic vulnerable to IP attacks).
